LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving

Wentao Zhu†, Ziao Sheng†, Peng Deng†, Huiqi Hu†∗, Xuan Zhou†, Xing Wei‡, Zhuang Wang‡ ††thanks: $ˆ∗$Corresponding author. Affiliation: †East China Normal University, ‡ZTE Corporation
†{wtzhu, 52315903002, 52295903003}@stu.ecnu.edu.cn, †{hqhu, xzhou}@dase.ecnu.edu.cn
‡{wei.xing6, wang.zhuang}@zte.com.cn
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels—external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests—and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85–0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path—leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged—and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4×\times larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache’s LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7–3.6×\times raw’s goodput and 1.9–3.1×\times lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7×\times via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31–1.34×\times as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw’s queue and goodput at 8. On a production-derived AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24×\times and 1.59×\times. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3’s numerical accuracy.

Index Terms: 
LLM serving, KV cache, lossless compression, tiered storage, GPU

I Introduction

Large language model (LLM) requests often share long prompt prefixes. An agent re-sends its growing transcript on every turn, while chat and retrieval-augmented (RAG) requests repeat history and documents [1, 2]. Processing these prefixes from scratch would repeat prefill work. Serving engines therefore retain their key/value (KV) cache so that returning requests can skip this computation. That cache is large. For instance, Qwen3-30B-A3B stores 96 KB of KV per token, and a GPU that reserves 32 GB for KV holds only five 64K-token agent sessions. Engines such as vLLM [3] and SGLang [4] therefore spill KV to host DRAM and SSD through external cache tiers (LMCache [5], Mooncake [6], SGLang HiCache [7], CachedAttention [8], Strata [9]) and load it back when a prefix returns.

Cache capacity affects serving performance at two levels: the external DRAM/SSD cache tiers and the GPU KV pool (§II-B). First, external cache capacity determines how much previously computed KV can be retained for reuse. When needed KV has been evicted, the engine must recompute it through prefill instead of loading it from cache. This increases computation and request latency. Second, GPU KV capacity limits how many long requests can run concurrently. Each active request needs space for its KV in the GPU pool. Even if its prefix is cached in DRAM or SSD, a request must wait when the GPU pool is full. Increasing external cache capacity does not provide this GPU space.

Thus, cache capacity matters at every level of the hierarchy. Storing KV in fewer bytes would add capacity at both places at once, without adding memory or drives. Most KV compression does so lossily: it quantizes values (KIVI [10], FP8 KV, CacheGen [11], KVTC [12]) or evicts tokens predicted to matter little (H2O [13], SnapKV [14]). Both change outputs, and accuracy must then be requalified per model and task.

Lossless compression can increase effective cache capacity without changing any KV value. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, the seven most frequent BF16 high-byte values per K or V tensor account for about 94% of high bytes on average (Fig. 1c). Because lossless compression preserves the stored representation exactly, it can also be applied to quantized formats such as FP8 KV.

We present LoomKV, which applies lossless compression to both the external cache tiers and the GPU KV pool. LoomKV supports two modes: tier mode and pool mode. In tier mode, DRAM and SSD store compressed KV, which is restored to its original form in the GPU pool before vLLM’s existing attention backend uses it. In pool mode, the GPU pool also stores compressed KV, and a custom decode-attention kernel reads and decompresses its compressed records as it computes attention.

In both modes, the question is whether the saved bytes become capacity. A compressed tier or pool holding BB bytes at stored ratio rr has B/rB/r raw-equivalent bytes. We call it capacity-equivalent if it performs like a raw one of that size. Achieving this equivalence requires preserving the space savings while keeping the overhead of compression and decompression low. This leads to five design requirements:

(i) Compression ratio: BF16 KV has limited redundancy, so the potential space savings from lossless compression are modest. Headers, indexes, and alignment padding must therefore be kept small to preserve those savings.

(ii) Reducing allocated space: in both modes, compression must reduce the memory or storage space allocated to the same amount of KV, so that the saved space can hold additional KV. Reserving the original uncompressed space for that KV would leave cache capacity unchanged.

(iii) Fast parallel decompression in tier mode: inference frameworks such as vLLM manage GPU KV in fixed-size pages, and a request’s pages need not be contiguous in GPU memory. When loading compressed KV from external cache tiers, decompression must exploit GPU parallelism to restore the original values directly into these pages at high throughput, avoiding an extra copy through a temporary buffer.

(iv) Fast attention in pool mode: each decode step must read KV directly from compressed GPU pages and recover the values needed for attention. The combined decompression and attention computation must match the speed of the engine’s existing kernels, FlashAttention-3 (FA3) [15] and FlashInfer [16].

(v) Avoiding synchronization stalls: when storing compressed KV in external cache tiers, the CPU must read the compressed KV sizes back from the GPU to allocate space and determine transfer sizes. This readback requires synchronization, but the wait must not block other KV cache loads.

We design LoomKV to meet these five requirements. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A lossless KV compression code (§IV; requirements i–ii): we design a lossless KV code in the same encoding family as ZipServ [17]. With calibrated codebooks, its tier-mode records use about 71% of the original BF16 KV storage across nine evaluated models, while preserving every KV value. To turn these savings into usable capacity, external tiers give each tier-mode record an object of its exact length, while the GPU pool packs variable-length pool-mode records into smaller fixed-size physical pages.

  • •

    Parallel GPU decompression in tier mode (§V; requirement iii): building on this encoding scheme, we design TileStream, a compressed KV layout that organizes bytes by type into separate data streams. Per-tile indexes locate the variable-length portions of these streams. Our GPU decompressor uses these indexes to decompress tiles in parallel, one per warp, and writes restored KV directly into the engine’s scattered cache pages, avoiding an intermediate copy.

  • •

    Fused decompression and decode attention (§VI, requirement iv): in pool mode, we design the FragPack layout and a kernel that fuses decompression with decode attention. FragPack packs compressed KV values in the order GPU threads need to form their operand fragments for matrix multiplication. Using this layout, the fused kernel decompresses each thread’s KV values directly into registers and immediately uses them in attention’s matrix multiplications, avoiding a separate pass that writes uncompressed KV back to GPU memory.

  • •

    Avoiding synchronization stalls in KV transfers (§VII; requirement v): we design a method that moves the CPU’s readback of GPU-computed lengths off the critical path when writing variable-length compressed KV to external cache tiers. This prevents the synchronization required for length readback from blocking other KV loads.

  • •

    Guidance for choosing a compression mode (§VIII, §IX): based on our evaluation of both modes, we give recommendations for selecting tier or pool mode using observations of system state. These recommendations help target the capacity bottleneck and avoid adding capacity where it does not improve serving performance.

We implement LoomKV on unmodified vLLM, with tier mode inside the cache server of LMCache [5] and pool mode as an out-of-tree attention backend. LMCache continues to manage allocation, eviction, write-through, and prefetch. We evaluate the two places where capacity limits service in turn, on the agent traces of AgentX [18]. First, tier mode achieves a compression ratio of about 71% for BF16 KV (compressed size divided by raw size). With 880 GB of DRAM and SSD combined, it matches the goodput of a raw deployment with 1231 GB. At the cliff of LMCache’s write-through LRU tiers, where raw tiers evict prefixes just before reuse, tier mode serves 2.7–3.6×\times raw’s goodput. Other policies move this cliff (§IX). Second, once the tiers hold the working set, a compressed GPU pool is capacity-equivalent at its token count: admitting 12 long requests at once, it has about the queue and goodput that a raw pool has with 8. Capacity also helps time-to-first-token (TTFT): hits move to faster tiers, cutting the TTFT of repeated prompts up to 1.7×\times. The cost is up to 2.2% of throughput where raw tiers suffice and about 2.5 GB of GPU memory per GPU in tier mode, and tier mode’s outputs are those of raw tiers, bit for bit.

II Background and Motivation

II-A KV cache management

The KV cache hierarchy spans GPU memory and external cache tiers. Inference frameworks commonly manage GPU KV memory as a pool of fixed-size pages. Pages are allocated as requests’ KV grows and reclaimed when no longer needed. A page table maps each request’s logical token blocks to physical pages, allowing attention to access KV stored at noncontiguous GPU addresses. External cache tiers retain reusable KV in DRAM (L1L_{1}) and SSD (L2L_{2}). When a prompt prefix is found in an external tier, its KV is loaded into GPU pages to avoid recomputing that prefix. These tiers manage allocation, eviction, and data transfers to preserve KV for reuse across requests.

II-B Where capacity limits service

For the measurements in Fig. 1, we serve Qwen3-30B-A3B on two H800 GPUs using vLLM and LMCache, with KV stored in uncompressed BF16. The AgentX workload consists of 64 live sessions sharing a 400 GB DRAM cache.

Panel (a) varies SSD capacity. Goodput counts requests per minute with engine time to first token ≤\leq 2 s and inter-token latency ≤\leq 40 ms. Reducing total DRAM and SSD capacity from 1200 GB to 1040 GB nearly halves goodput, from 9.4 to 4.6 requests per minute, as cached KV is evicted before reuse. This capacity cliff contrasts with the smaller gains at larger capacities, where goodput begins to level off. Additional results for these two configurations (not plotted in panel (a)) show the hit rate falling from 0.84 to 0.55.

Panel (b) fixes SSD capacity at 2 TB and uses admission limits of 8, 12, and 16. It shows that GPU KV capacity can limit concurrency even when the external tiers hold the working set. Raising the admission limit from 12 to 16 increases the mean number of running requests by only 0.8, but adds 2.9 waiting requests. Goodput, shown by the labels above the bars, falls from 10.6 to 3.7 requests per minute despite the higher admission limit. Increasing external cache capacity cannot resolve this GPU-space bottleneck.

These results identify two distinct capacity bottlenecks. External cache capacity limits KV reuse: when the tiers become too small to retain KV until reuse, evictions force recomputation instead of fast DRAM or SSD loads and can trigger a goodput cliff. GPU KV capacity limits concurrency: even with cache hits, requests must wait when the GPU pool is full. Capacity should therefore be added at the level that limits KV reuse or request concurrency.

II-C Where the compressible bits are

Fig. 1c summarizes all 48 layers of Qwen3-30B-A3B, each with one key (K) tensor and one value (V) tensor. We split each BF16 value into a high byte and a low byte. Within each tensor, we rank the 256 possible values of each byte separately by frequency, then average the share of occurrences in each rank group across the 96 tensors. The high byte holds the sign bit and upper seven exponent bits. On average, its seven most frequent values account for about 94% of occurrences, and the top 14 account for 99.81%, leaving 0.19% for the remaining 242 values. For the low byte, the top seven and top 14 values account for only 4.21% and 8.21%, respectively. We observe a similar pattern in the other models we evaluated. This concentration makes the high byte the main target for lossless compression to increase effective KV cache capacity.

II-D Why not existing GPU compression methods

General-purpose compression. Libraries such as nvCOMP [19] offer GPU compression and decompression of data blocks across applications. These compressors are not specifically designed for KV caches. We compare nvCOMP’s ANS, Bitcomp and LZ4 implementations with LoomKV on the same KV data and GPU (Table II). They save less space and restore paged KV more slowly; nvCOMP ANS stores 72.5% of raw bytes and restores at 182 GB/s, versus 70.9% and 1182 GB/s for LoomKV.

Offline weight compression. DFloat11, ZipNN and ZipServ [20, 21, 17] compress static model weights offline to reduce their storage footprint. ZipServ also fuses decompression with matrix multiplication (GEMM). KV is generated online and consumed from paged caches by attention, so these weight-oriented workflows and kernels cannot be used directly.

Transfer-oriented KV compression. SplitZip [22] reduces communication between prefill and decode workers by compressing KV for transfer. It decompresses into a contiguous buffer at 1215 GB/s. It then needs a separate pass to scatter the KV into the engine’s cache pages. On the same KV data and GPU, SplitZip stores 76.8% of the raw bytes and restores paged KV at 671 GB/s. LoomKV stores 70.9% and restores KV directly into the pages at 1182 GB/s (Table II).

Compression must also reduce allocated cache space; shorter outputs alone do not increase usable capacity.

III System Overview

Two modes. LoomKV supports two modes sharing the lossless encoding scheme of §IV. In tier mode (Fig. 2a), the inference engine keeps uncompressed KV in its GPU pool and uses its existing attention backend. The KV cache server compresses KV for storage in DRAM or SSD and restores its original bits when loading it into the GPU pool. This increases external cache capacity while preserving model execution and the cache server’s tier management (§V).

In pool mode (Fig. 2b), the inference engine keeps its GPU KV pool compressed and reads it through a backend that fuses decompression with decode attention (§VI), increasing GPU KV capacity. Compression preserves every bit of the stored KV. The fused attention kernel uses a different summation order from the original backend, so its outputs may differ slightly due to floating-point rounding (§VIII-G).

KV records. In Fig. 2, a record is the unit of compressed KV. Its granularity and layout depend on how the GPU decompresses it. In tier mode, the cache server loads a whole chunk into GPU global memory on a hit. One TileStream record therefore contains both K and V for a block of 128 tokens across all layers.

In pool mode, each chunk has two FragPack records per KV head in each layer, one for K and one for V. The attention kernel uses the K record to compute attention weights and the V record to accumulate the output. This granularity lets a thread block stage whole compressed records in the limited shared memory of a streaming multiprocessor (SM). FragPack orders the data by the threads that consume them, so each thread can decompress its operands directly into registers for attention.

Data paths (Fig. 2). The cache server is a separate process that reaches the engine’s blocks through CUDA IPC, so its kernels read and write them directly. In tier mode, the engine’s connector asks the server to store a chunk after the step that completes it. The server compresses the chunk into a GPU buffer , copies the TileStream record into L1L_{1}  and also writes it to L2L_{2} , because the server writes every object to both tiers (write-through). On a lookup, the server returns the longest prefix it holds and prefetches chunks held only in L2L_{2} into L1L_{1} . A load copies the records into GPU buffers  and decompresses them into the engine’s blocks .

In pool mode, the K and V of new tokens are first kept raw in a staging buffer. When a block is complete, the attention backend compresses it into pages of the pool, and attention reads these pages directly. A store and a load take the same steps as in tier mode, but the cache server compresses nothing. It groups the FragPack records of a complete block into one cache object in a GPU buffer  and, on a load, imports them into the pool’s pages , so the tiers hold the pool’s records unchanged. In both modes, only compressed bytes cross PCIe.

The next four sections describe the code and its allocation (§IV), TileStream and its decompressor (§V), FragPack and fused attention (§VI), and transfers without synchronization stalls (§VII).

IV A Lossless KV Code

Both modes of LoomKV share a lossless code that stores each BF16 scalar’s low byte verbatim and replaces its high byte with a fixed-width symbol indexing a static codebook.

IV-A Symbols, codebooks, and calibration

Byte-aligned, fixed-width symbols. Because the BF16 low byte carries 7.97 bits of entropy out of 8, LoomKV stores it verbatim. For the high byte, LoomKV codes all eight bits together rather than isolating the 8-bit exponent as SplitZip [22] does: because the exponent straddles the high and low bytes, coding only the exponent shrinks records by only about 0.3% while breaking byte alignment and adding bit-shift and reassembly instructions on every scalar.

LoomKV also avoids variable-length entropy codes such as Huffman coding and asymmetric numeral systems (ANS). Because a GPU warp executes 32 lanes in lockstep, fast decompression requires every lane to read its symbols at fixed offsets and execute identical lookup instructions. Under a variable-length code, each symbol’s bit offset depends on all preceding symbols; even interleaved multi-stream variants [23] still decompress several times slower on GPUs than fixed-width lookups.

Two-level 3-bit code. Each high byte receives a 3-bit primary symbol: values 0–6 index the seven most frequent high bytes in the codebook’s first row, and value 7 is an escape. We choose three bits because wider symbols (such as 4 bits) would spend an extra bit on every scalar even though the top seven values already cover roughly 94% of high bytes, and eight 1-byte entries fit the 8-byte register input of a single GPU byte-permute instruction (PRMT). Because about 6% of high bytes escape the first row, writing an 8-bit raw byte on every primary escape would add 0.06×8=0.480.06\times 8=0.48 bits per scalar; each primary escape instead emits a 3-bit secondary symbol indexing the next seven frequent values in the codebook’s second row. Only when a high byte falls outside all 14 entries does secondary symbol 7 escape to a verbatim 8-bit raw byte (0.19% of high bytes). Fig. 3 traces this code on eight BF16 scalars: low bytes stay verbatim, common high bytes (3C, 3B) map directly to primary symbols 0 and 3, 39 escapes once to secondary symbol 0, and rare 41 escapes twice to a raw byte. Pool mode widens the second level to 4 bits (15 secondary entries) to keep fused decompression loop-free (§VI-A).

Per-head codebooks and calibration. Sharing one global codebook across all KV loses compression because each layer’s K and V tensors have different exponent ranges, whereas per-channel codebooks add negligible entropy gain while forcing lanes to switch codebooks across channels. Because adjacent scalars handled by a lane belong to the same KV head within one layer’s K or V tensor, LoomKV keeps one codebook per KV head in each layer’s K or V tensor—the finest granularity at which each lane consults a single codebook. Codebooks remain static after server startup: LoomKV provides a generic fallback codebook and calibrates model-specific codebooks offline from a single 1024-token forward pass, storing a codebook digest in record headers to prevent mismatches. One offline calibration generalizes across prompt domains and sequence lengths.

Extension to FP8 KV. For 8-bit FP8 (E4M3) KV, the same two-level code stores the three mantissa bits verbatim and codes the upper five bits (sign and exponent) with FP8 codebooks. Because FP8 channel magnitudes vary within a head, LoomKV subtracts a static per-channel integer exponent offset before compression and adds it back during decompression so all channels within a head share one codebook. Since rotary position embeddings (RoPE) rotate K channel pairs with token position, offline calibration re-rotates captured K tensors across the model’s 256K context before fitting K’s offsets; BF16 KV needs no per-channel offsets and thus no RoPE re-rotation.

IV-B From saved bytes to capacity

Compressed records vary in byte length with their escape counts, whereas external cache tiers and GPU KV pools are provisioned around fixed-size units. Each mode converts saved bytes into capacity to match its allocator.

Exact-length tier objects. In tier mode, the KV cache server treats the raw chunk size only as an upper bound: once GPU compression yields a record’s actual byte length, the server allocates an L1L_{1} DRAM object of that exact length and writes it unchanged to L2L_{2} SSD. On L2L_{2} write completion, the server records the compressed length in host metadata so later prefetches from L2L_{2} reserve exact-sized L1L_{1} buffers before issuing SSD reads. Neither the variable-size L1L_{1} allocator nor byte-based LRU eviction requires changes.

Smaller fixed-size GPU pages. Pool mode preserves the engine’s fixed-size page-table layout so GPU memory management stays unchanged, but shrinks each physical page to cover the typical compressed length of a block’s records, yielding proportionally more KV blocks from the same GPU budget (§VI-A).

V Tier Mode: TileStream and Parallel Decompression

In tier mode, the KV cache server compresses each chunk into a TileStream record and decompresses fetched records straight into the inference engine’s scattered GPU pages.

V-A The TileStream layout

Whole record (Fig. 4a). On Qwen3-30B-A3B, one TileStream record holds 96 K/V tensors (one K and one V per layer across 48 layers) behind a 4 KB-aligned header of per-tensor offsets (V, layer 0 expanded in panel b), followed by 4 KB padding for O_DIRECT SSD transfers. Incompressible chunks fall back to raw storage so worst-case size never exceeds raw KV. Kernels address engine blocks through strides to accommodate different engine K/V layouts and execute independently per tensor-parallel (TP) rank (12 MB raw full-model chunk on Qwen3-30B-A3B, or 6 MB per rank at TP 2).

Streams and grouped tile index (Fig. 4b). Each K/V tensor groups bytes by type into four contiguous streams—low bytes, primary symbols, secondary symbols, and raw bytes—so GPU threads read fixed-width data via coalesced loads while isolating variable-length escapes to the last two streams. Each tensor splits into 256-scalar tiles (256 tiles per 4-head tensor on Qwen3-30B-A3B, or 128 per rank at TP 2): one GPU lane reads or writes eight BF16 scalars in a single 128-bit vector instruction (16 B; 64-bit for FP8), so a 32-lane warp naturally covers 32×8=25632\times 8=256 scalars as one tile. While a tile’s low-byte and primary offsets are fixed, its secondary and raw offsets depend on all prior escapes. To let warps decompress tiles in parallel without scanning earlier tiles, each K/V tensor appends a grouped tile index. Storing two 32-bit prefix counts per tile would cost 0.25 bits/scalar; grouping eight tiles (32 groups per tensor) halves this to 0.14 bits/scalar (36 B/group): two 32-bit base counts (Σs,Σr\Sigma_{s},\Sigma_{r}) for tile 0 plus seven 32-bit words packing 16-bit group-relative secondary and raw offsets for tiles 1–7. Fig. 4b shows the first 8-tile group alongside full-tensor totals (64, 24, 1.5, 0.12, and 1.1 KB): to reach tile 3, a warp computes its fixed low/primary positions and adds word 3 to (Σs,Σr\Sigma_{s},\Sigma_{r}) to jump straight to tile 3’s secondary and raw slices (arrows).

Stored size and bit budget (Fig. 4c). The streams and the index of one tensor add up to 90.7 KB of its 128 KB raw size. Per scalar, the low-byte and primary streams cost a fixed 8 and 3 bits, and the secondary stream, the raw stream, and the index add 3​pe+8​pr+0.143p_{e}+8p_{r}+0.14 bits. At Qwen3-30B-A3B’s measured escape rates (pe=0.061p_{e}=0.061, pr=0.0019p_{r}=0.0019), escapes and the index add only 0.34 bits, totaling 11.34 of 16 bits (ratio 0.709, saving 4.66 bits) with under 1% metadata and alignment overhead.

V-B Parallel decompressor

During a load, each warp decompresses one 256-scalar tile directly into the engine’s scattered KV pages, with each of its 32 lanes handling eight adjacent scalars from one KV head. Fig. 5 traces one lane through four steps (with branchless lookup):

1. Mark escapes. The lane loads its eight 3-bit primary symbols as one 24-bit word and unpacks them into eight 4-bit nibbles (matching PRMT’s 4-bit selector width). Bitwise-ANDing the three value bits of each nibble flags every primary escape (symbol 7 at positions 2 and 5) and counts escapes locally without cross-lane communication.

2. Warp scan. Two warp-level exclusive prefix sums over the lanes’ primary- and secondary-escape counts, added to the tile’s index offsets (Σs,Σr\Sigma_{s},\Sigma_{r}), give each lane its exact positions in the secondary and raw streams (Fig. 5b), from which it loads up to one 24-bit secondary word and any needed raw bytes.

3. Branchless PRMT lookup. Each head’s codebook is repacked into 16 B in registers: primary values in bytes 0–6, secondary values in bytes 8–14, and 00 in escape slots 7 and 15. A first PRMT lookup resolves all non-escaped primary symbols while writing 00 at escaped slots (Fig. 5a); a second PRMT pass resolves secondary symbols, merges any raw bytes, and uses a rank PRMT to place them into the escaped slots with 00 elsewhere (Fig. 5b). A single bitwise OR produces all eight high bytes with zero branch divergence.

4. Reassemble and direct write. The lane loads its eight verbatim low bytes, interleaves them with the decompressed high bytes in registers (for FP8, it adds per-channel offsets and reattaches the 3-bit mantissa), and writes the eight scalars straight into the engine’s target KV page (Fig. 5c), avoiding any staging buffer or scatter pass. To guard against corrupt records, write addresses come exclusively from host-validated metadata and all record-derived read offsets are clamped to the load buffer.

V-C Direct-from-pages compressor

On the store path, three consecutive GPU kernels compress a batch of chunks with no host synchronization between them: a count kernel reads KV directly from the engine’s paged blocks and tallies per-tile escapes, a single-cooperative-thread-array (CTA) layout kernel computes stream offsets and flags incompressible chunks for raw fallback, and a compact kernel writes the aligned header, streams, and tile index into the store buffer. Reading directly from paged blocks instead of first gathering chunks into a contiguous buffer saves two full passes over raw KV and roughly two kernel launches per chunk, reducing both memory traffic and GPU time-slice contention with the inference engine.

VI Pool Mode: FragPack and Fused Decode Attention

In pool mode, the inference engine stores compressed FragPack records directly in its GPU KV pool, and an out-of-tree attention backend plugin computes decode attention over them without engine source changes.

VI-A FragPack records and compressed pages

Granularity and MMA fragment order. Each FragPack record holds 128×128128\times 128 scalars (32 KB raw; Fig. 6a) for one 128-token block, layer, KV head, and tensor (K or V). The fused kernel runs 256-thread (8-warp) CTAs, each over a run of consecutive pages of one request and KV head, and feeds every record it reads to tensor-core matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) instructions, where each thread supplies a fixed 64-scalar fragment of the record from registers. FragPack permutes scalars at compression time into this per-thread fragment order (K in row order, V in transposed order V⊤V^{\top}), so every thread fetches its bytes via wide, coalesced loads indexed solely by thread ID.

Two-part layout and 4-bit secondary level. Each record pairs a fixed-length dense part—16 384 B of low bytes plus 6144 B of 3-bit primary symbols (22 528 B)—with a variable part capped at 2 KB so escapes stage in a fixed shared-memory buffer (records exceeding this cap fall back to raw). Because each of the CTA’s eight warps always decompresses its own fixed 2048 scalars, FragPack needs no tile index; an eight-entry per-warp prefix header suffices to locate every warp’s secondary and raw slices. As expanded in Fig. 6a, the variable part holds this header, 4-bit secondary nibbles (15 codebook entries plus escape 15), and 4-byte raw entries (each storing a raw high byte and its escape position). Widening the second level to 4 bits (3+4) keeps fused decompression loop-free: each of a warp’s 32 lanes patches at most one raw scalar (capping warps at 32 raw scalars before raw fallback). On captured Qwen3-30B-A3B KV, 4-bit nibbles cut raw scalars from 25 to 0.3 per record (max ≤10\leq 10 per warp, 0% cap-induced fallback vs. 0.2% with 3 bits) at +0.1% record size; the variable part averages 550 B and never exceeds 1872 B.

Shared-budget pages, overflow, and record map. Each compressed GPU page holds 2​H2H records for one block and layer (H=4⇒8H=4\Rightarrow 8 records in Fig. 6b). Rather than reserving the worst-case 2 KB per record, the 2​H2H records share a pooled variable budget of 1280 B per record (above Qwen3-30B-A3B’s fullest page at 1140 B/record and well above the 395–562 B means across nine grouped-query attention (GQA) models). For H=4H=4, a page shrinks from 262 144 B to 190 464 B, yielding 1.38×1.38\times as many blocks before deducting backend working buffers.

When a block finishes, its 2​H2H records compress in parallel and claim space in arbitrary completion order (K1, V0, K0, K3, V1, K2, V3 in Fig. 6b) by advancing a per-page fill counter via atomic compare-and-swap (CAS); if a record exceeds the remaining space, it aborts without advancing the counter so shorter records can still fit. Records that overflow the page or exceed the compression limits are stored raw (32 KB) in a shared overflow area (V2 in Fig. 6b); in Qwen3-30B-A3B serving runs, only 0.03% of records fall back to raw (0.009% from full pages). A per-layer record map stores each record’s (address, length), pointing directly into either its page or an overflow slot. Storing the variable-part length for compressed records and 32 KB for raw records lets attention detect raw fallback via length >2>2 KB and read every record directly without computing page-internal offsets.

VI-B Fused decompression and decode attention

Because each decode step emits one token per request while reading the entire context’s KV, decompressing into a workspace first would write and re-read all raw bytes every step. LoomKV instead decompresses each FragPack record straight into registers for tensor-core MMAs, reading ≈0.70\approx 0.70 of raw KV bytes and never writing decompressed KV back to GPU memory.

Three-stage CTA dataflow and pipelining (Fig. 6c). Inside one CTA, each page’s K and V records flow across GPU memory, shared memory, registers, and tensor cores in three stages: (1) Aligned TMA staging: the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) copies each record’s exact byte length asynchronously into a dedicated shared-memory K or V slot. Because TMA penalizes unaligned 128-byte transfers, matching the slot’s address remainder modulo 128 to the source address avoids a ≈30%\approx 30\% bandwidth penalty. (2) Register decompression: each thread decompresses its 64 scalars into registers via PRMT primary lookup, warp-scan escape lookup, and loop-free 4-bit secondary/raw patching (skipping decompression on raw records for bitwise identical output), yielding KiK_{i} and transposed Vi⊤V_{i}^{\top} directly in MMA fragment order. (3) Tensor-core MMAs and online softmax: using m16n8k16 MMAs (C+=A​BC\mathrel{+}=AB), the K step multiplies KiK_{i} (in AA) by the eight GQA query heads (in BB) to obtain scores S⊤=K​Q⊤S^{\top}=KQ^{\top} and online-softmax BF16 weights PP. Because warps partition 16 tokens in the K step but 16 output dimensions across all 128 tokens in the V step, the CTA exchanges PP through shared memory before accumulating O⊤+=V⊤​P⊤O^{\top}\mathrel{+}=V^{\top}P^{\top} in registers.

Dual K/V shared-memory slots keep TMA one record ahead of computation across the CTA’s pages (K0, V0, K1, V1, K2, V2, bottom of Fig. 6c): TMA fetches V0 while threads process K0 and fetches K1 once K0’s slot retires, hiding copy latency behind decompression and MMAs.

Prefill. Because prefill is compute-dominated rather than KV-read dominated, pool mode leaves prefill unfused: it decompresses cached pages into a temporary BF16 workspace and runs the engine’s stock attention kernel, adding at most 3% to prefill time.

VI-C Open blocks and CUDA graphs

Open blocks. Only complete 128-token blocks are compressed; each running request keeps its in-progress open block raw in a per-request staging buffer that attention reads alongside the compressed pages. Before each step, a lightweight host hook reads scheduler metadata to update request block lists, recycle finished staging buffers, assign buffers to newly opened blocks, and populate a fixed-capacity list of blocks hitting token 128. During the step, each layer compresses those newly completed blocks right after attention (one CTA per record).

CUDA graph compatibility. Serving engines replay full decode steps as single CUDA graphs, which requires kernel grids and argument buffers to stay fixed for a given padded batch shape. Because per-step attention scheduling computes CTA work assignments on the GPU and block compression reads the fixed-capacity list populated outside the graph, all per-layer launch parameters depend solely on padded batch shape, preserving full CUDA-graph capture and replay.

VII Avoiding Synchronization Stalls in KV Transfers

The KV cache server executes all stores and loads for a GPU on one handler thread. Variable-length compression creates two stall hazards: reading GPU-computed compressed lengths back to the host would block queued loads on the handler thread, and multi-process GPU time-slice waits during decompression would stall PCIe transfers if copies and decompression shared a single buffer. Fig. 7 shows how LoomKV eliminates both stalls.

VII-A Store path: deferred length readback

To move length readback off the handler thread, LoomKV splits stores across two threads (Fig. 7a). For each batch of uncached chunks (up to 32), the handler claims a GPU store buffer, launches the three-kernel compressor (§V-C), records a CUDA event, hands the batch to a background store worker, and immediately returns to serve queued loads. On its own CPU thread and CUDA stream, the store worker waits on the event, reads all batch lengths in one host synchronization, allocates exact-length L1L_{1} objects, copies the records into L1L_{1}, and triggers the server’s write-through to L2L_{2}. If all store buffers fill under bursts, the handler applies backpressure until one frees rather than dropping stores.

VII-B Load path: overlapped copies and decompression

Because host metadata already holds each pinned L1L_{1} object’s exact length, loads need no length readback and run directly on the handler thread, skipping chunks already present in the engine’s local prefix cache. To prevent multi-process GPU compute time-slice waits from stalling PCIe DMA (which does not wait for compute slices), LoomKV pipelines PCIe copies and GPU decompression on two CUDA streams rotating through a ring of GPU load buffers (four in our deployment; Fig. 7b). Each decompression waits via a CUDA event only on its own buffer’s copy, and each buffer refill waits only on that buffer’s prior decompression, hiding time-slice pauses behind continuous PCIe transfers. Kernel launch descriptors are cached once per batch shape. When a batch includes an incompressible raw chunk, or when its first chunk lies partly inside the engine’s local prefix-cache hit so only the remaining tokens may be written, LoomKV falls back to decompressing into a scratch buffer and scattering via the server’s stock transfer kernel.

VII-C Extending both paths to pool mode

Pool mode reuses both asynchronous pipelines with three localized changes: (1) Object format: each cache object bundles all layers’ FragPack records for one complete 128-token block behind a 4 KB-aligned header (KV shape, codebook digest, record lengths), keeping one uniform representation across GPU, L1L_{1}, and L2L_{2} (requiring chunk size = block size = 128). (2) Store path: an export kernel replaces compression, gathering records from pool pages or overflow into a store buffer; deferred length readback, L1L_{1} copy, and L2L_{2} write-through stay unchanged. (3) Load path: an import kernel replaces decompression, validating headers, packing records into pool pages via atomic fill counters (§VI-A), and publishing record-map entries. Because corrupt headers or a full overflow area can fail an import, the handler performs one status readback after queueing all imports for the request—avoiding mid-pipeline stalls—and the engine recomputes any failed batch.

VIII Evaluation

We evaluate LoomKV around six questions, one per subsection:

Q1: how much space does the code save across models and workloads?

Q2: are its compression, decompression, and fused-attention kernels fast enough to stay off the critical path?

Q3: how much does tier mode improve goodput and TTFT when external cache tiers are short of space?

Q4: how much does pool mode improve them when the GPU KV pool limits concurrency?

Q5: do both modes also help on a second production-derived workload?

Q6: what overheads does compression introduce, and which outputs remain exact?

VIII-A Setup

This subsection describes the shared serving testbed used across our main AgentX experiments; setup details specific to the code microbenchmarks, kernel benchmarks, and the second workload appear in Q1, Q2, and Q5.

Hardware and models. The server has 1 TB of DRAM, 15 TB of SSD, and two H800 GPUs (80 GB, 700 W). Unless noted, we serve Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct at TP 2 (mixture-of-experts, MoE; 96 KB of BF16 KV per token), alongside GLM-4-9B-Chat-1M (dense, 80 KB/token). Q1 additionally evaluates stored KV ratios across nine dense and MoE models from 4B to 72B parameters. The inference engine is unmodified vLLM 0.30 with 128-token blocks and FA3 as its stock attention backend.

Cache server and baselines. Every serving configuration runs LMCache 0.5.6 with 128-token chunks, bounded DRAM (L1L_{1}) and SSD (L2L_{2}) tiers, and LRU eviction. The raw BF16 baseline runs unmodified LMCache; the lossy baseline configures vLLM with uncompressed FP8 KV (halving KV size in both the GPU pool and external tiers). In Q2, we additionally benchmark LoomKV’s kernels against SplitZip, ExANS, and three nvCOMP compressors (ANS, Bitcomp, LZ4), and compare offline sizes with ZipServ and ZipFusion.

Main workload. Our primary serving workload is AgentX [18], replaying the 393 Claude Code sessions of cc-traces [24] as session trees with subagents and recorded think times; all reported metrics cover only the profiling window after warm-up. Sessions share no prefix, and prompts reach 254K tokens (median 89K). Each GPU reserves 54 GB for KV (1.18 M raw tokens); in pool mode, the staging buffers, overflow area, and record map are deducted from this same 54 GB budget.

Admission and metrics. Because the harness keeps one request in flight per live session, a FIFO proxy in front of vLLM admits at most SS requests concurrently so engine queueing does not mask cache effects. We default to S=8S=8, which keeps the raw GPU pool free of internal queueing (Q4 sweeps SS to 16). We report engine TTFT (harness TTFT minus proxy wait), goodput (requests/min meeting engine TTFT ≤2\leq 2 s and inter-token latency (ITL) ≤40\leq 40 ms), hit rate (share of prompt tokens served from cache), and throughput (prompt tokens/s).

Sizing and repeats. With SS fixed, live sessions PP set the reused working set WW (306 GB raw at P=32P=32; 641 GB at P=64P=64). Most experiments use P=64P=64, 400 GB DRAM, and SSD caps from 400 GB to 2 TB over an 1800 s profiling window (≈600\approx 600 requests). We run every experiment three times and report the median (each end-to-end table row is the median-goodput run). Where tiers hold the working set, repeats vary by roughly 1% in throughput and 4% in goodput; near a capacity cliff, we also report the full repeat range.

VIII-B Q1: Compression ratio

Across all nine models, LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.70–0.71 of its raw size, staying within 0.033–0.036 of the order-0 entropy bound.

Cross-model compression ratio. Table I shows that calibrated TileStream records compress BF16 KV tightly and uniformly across all nine Qwen, Llama, and GLM models (0.705–0.709, within 0.033–0.036 of the order-0 bound). On Qwen3-30B-A3B, this 0.709 ratio breaks down into 0.676 entropy, 0.024 fixed-width symbol overhead, and 0.009 for the grouped tile index and 4 KB-aligned header. Calibration improves every model over the generic fallback (most visibly on Qwen3-30B-A3B, from 0.764 to 0.709), and compresses FP8 KV to 0.853–0.873. FragPack reaches slightly tighter BF16 ratios (0.700–0.705) because its per-warp header is smaller than a tile index, and its variable part stays well under the 1280 B per-record page budget across every model (var. B in Table I); on held-out FP8 agent KV up to 240K tokens, FragPack compresses to 0.838.

Workload and context-length stability. Calibrated codebooks depend on the model rather than the prompt domain or sequence position. One offline forward pass over 1024 tokens produces them, and they occupy 8.4 KB on Qwen3-30B-A3B (22 B for each layer, K or V, and KV head; FP8 adds 48 KB of per-channel exponent offsets). Codebooks calibrated on one agent session store prose, source code, Chinese chat, math, synthetic needles, and random tokens at 0.706–0.709 BF16—within 0.001 of domain-specific calibrations (and within 0.018 for FP8, at 0.852–0.871)—and stay flat at 0.709–0.710 across every position of a 240K-token context.

Design choices (Fig. 8). Panel (a) explains why our fixed-width code approaches the 2.85-bit order-0 entropy bound: two-level 3+3 (3.20 bits/high byte) beats every alternative—6% fewer bits than ZipServ [17], 8% fewer than single-level 3+raw, 20% fewer than ALP-RD’s positioned exceptions [25], and 25% fewer than SplitZip’s 4-bit exponent code with 56-bit out-of-band exceptions [22]. Pool mode’s 3+4 adds only 1.2% to high-byte bits (+0.1% to total FragPack record size) while enabling loop-free fused decompression. Panel (b) justifies per-head codebooks: moving from one global codebook to per-layer K/V tensors captures almost all BF16 entropy gain across both models, per-head stays flat, and per-channel adds no benefit (slightly overfitting held-out Qwen3 KV). For FP8, subtracting static per-channel exponent offsets lets per-head codebooks match per-channel bounds on Qwen3 (0.795 vs. 0.795) and close roughly half the remaining gap on GLM-4 (0.810 vs. 0.794).

VIII-C Q2: Kernels

LoomKV’s kernels keep compression and decompression off the critical path in both modes: TileStream decompresses paged blocks at 81% of raw copy speed and hides behind PCIe copies under GPU contention, while FragPack’s fused BF16 decode kernel outperforms both FA3 and FlashInfer on nearly every batch shape.

Tier-mode compression and decompression. Table II benchmarks single-GPU throughput with byte-for-byte verification. On stores, LoomKV compresses directly from paged blocks 1.6×\times faster than SplitZip and 4.7–59×\times faster than ExANS and nvCOMP. On loads, writing straight from registers into scattered KV pages achieves 81% of raw paged copy speed—an order of magnitude above PCIe bandwidth—avoiding the extra scatter pass that nearly halves contiguous-only SplitZip’s throughput while storing 8% fewer bytes. Variable-length ANS decompressors (ExANS, nvCOMP ANS) run 6.3×\times slower despite ExANS’s 1.6% tighter ratio; general-purpose Bitcomp saves little space; and LZ4 finds no byte-level matches in interleaved BF16 (ratio 1.0005, stored raw). Offline size comparisons with ZipServ and ZipFusion confirm the same compression margin (Table II).

Overlapped loads beside a busy engine. In serving, LMCache shares the GPU with vLLM as a separate process, so decompression can interfere with inference [28]. Without CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS), decompression kernels wait for GPU compute time slices whereas PCIe DMA copies do not. Loading a 110K-token prefix while another process saturates the GPU with BF16 matrix multiplications exposes this stall: with one load buffer, every PCIe copy waits for the prior decompression to get a time slice, inflating latency to 288–294 ms (more than double raw copies at 117–141 ms). Rotating four load buffers cuts latency to 90 ms—close to 83 ms with one buffer on an idle GPU and matching PCIe transfer time for 0.71 of the raw bytes—keeping decompression hidden behind PCIe transfers.

Pool-mode fused decode attention. Fig. 9 compares our fused BF16 decode kernel against FA3 (as configured by vLLM; FA3’s own default differs by at most 1%) and FlashInfer [16] at full GPU clock. The fused kernel wins on every shape except one: at TP 1 it runs at 0.80–0.92×\times FlashInfer’s time and 0.56–0.85×\times FA3’s; on a TP 2 rank it runs at 0.79–0.97×\times FlashInfer on 11 of 12 shapes (only 1×\times32K rises to 1.23×\times, where FlashInfer stays flat from 8K). Running the same kernel over raw FragPack records takes 0.90–0.96×\times FlashInfer on multi-request TP 1 batches, showing that speedups come from both kernel design and reading 30% fewer KV bytes.

Under sustained AgentX serving, both H800 GPUs sit at their 700 W power cap in over 99% of busy samples. Under continuous execution (reaching the 700 W cap on all larger batches), BF16 keeps its lead: the fused kernel takes 0.84–0.95×\times FlashInfer’s time at TP 1 (FA3 takes 1.03–1.19×\times) and 0.82–0.98×\times at TP 2, except 1×\times32K (1.35×\times). Aligning each record’s shared-memory slot with its source address modulo 128 cuts the fused kernel’s time at the cap by 3–6%, with bit-identical outputs. On FP8 KV, however, the fused kernel loses its lead at the cap (0.98–1.15×\times FlashInfer and 1.21–1.30×\times FA3 above 32K tokens). Unfused prefill decompression adds at most 3% over FA3 alone.

VIII-D Q3: Compressed cache tiers

A compressed cache tier behaves like a raw tier with 1.4×1.4\times its capacity—the inverse of the 0.71 stored ratio. Between raw’s LRU cliff and compressed’s cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7–3.6×\times raw’s goodput; where raw already fits the working set, tier mode matches it.

SSD capacity sweep and cliff dynamics (Fig. 10a, Table III). Sweeping SSD capacity from 2 TB down to 400 GB shifts the LRU cliff leftward by ≈1.4×\approx 1.4\times: raw LMCache falls off its cliff below 1200 GB while tier mode sustains near-peak goodput down to 640 GB. Between the two cliffs, tier mode delivers 2.8–2.9×\times raw’s goodput at 640 GB and 2.7–3.6×\times across repeats at 480 GB, cutting mean engine TTFT by 1.9–3.1×\times (Table III reports representative points; Fig. 10 plots the full sweep). Inside raw’s cliff at 640 GB, tier mode holds its hit rate steady near 0.90 across the 30-minute window whereas raw decays continuously to 0.17 as prefixes evict shortly before reuse; recomputing 45% of prompt tokens pushes raw’s p90 TTFT from 2.8 s to 19 s (tier mode: 3.4 s) and ITL from 26 to 44 ms, leaving 63% of raw requests within the 2 s target versus 79% for tier mode. Outside the cliff region, gains taper as expected (1.2–1.4×\times at 800 GB where raw recovers, and 1.3×\times at 400 GB where neither holds the working set). The gain is insensitive to the service-level objective (SLO) definition: at 640 GB, tier mode serves 2.5–2.9×\times raw’s goodput across TTFT targets from 1 s to 10 s, and 2.3–2.4×\times with no ITL target. On GLM-4-9B (whose KV is 0.83 of Qwen3’s bytes/token), the cliff occurs at smaller SSD sizes, yielding 3.8×\times raw’s goodput at 400 GB (Table III). Storing BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size also cuts the bytes each chunk moves over PCIe and writes to the SSD by 29%, so every byte written to the drive holds 1.4×1.4\times as much KV.

Capacity equivalence (Fig. 10b). Replotting every run by raw-equivalent DRAM plus SSD bytes (dividing tier mode’s physical bytes by 0.709 on Qwen3 and 0.707 on GLM-4) collapses both modes onto a single curve on both models. Three enlarged-tier raw controls (hollow diamonds) verify this directly: tier mode at 880 GB physical (1241 raw-equivalent GB, serving 9.3–12.5 req/min across repeats) matches a proportionally enlarged 1231 GB raw control (10.7 req/min), and enlarging only SSD (1072 GB) or only DRAM (1200 GB) falls on the exact same curve. Total DRAM plus SSD governs even under write-through because the two tiers evict independently and DRAM hits do not refresh SSD timestamps, allowing DRAM to retain objects already evicted from SSD.

Faster-tier promotion (Fig. 10c). Splitting hits by serving tier reveals two effects. First, raw collapses at the cliff because SSD hits vanish as objects evict before reuse, driving mean TTFT up sharply. Second, expanding L1L_{1} DRAM by ≈1.4×\approx 1.4\times promotes hits upward from SSD into DRAM at every SSD size (raising DRAM’s share from 0.36–0.41 to 0.52–0.59), lowering median engine TTFT even at 2 TB (0.99 s to 0.89 s). In a controlled 48-prompt repeat trace (8K–128K tokens, 261 GB raw vs. 188 GB compressed), this SSD-to-DRAM promotion cuts second-pass TTFT by 1.6–1.7×\times at 220 GB DRAM (matching 400 GB raw; 1.3–1.4×\times at 160 GB) while keeping cold first-pass latency within 2% from 32K upward.

Single-tier DRAM-only sweep (Fig. 11). Removing SSD reproduces the same equivalence: varying live sessions PP on 400 GB DRAM shifts the sustainable session count by 1.2–1.5×\times (centered on 1.4×\times). Across the shaded cliff bands, tier mode delivers 3.5–4.3×\times raw’s goodput on Qwen3-30B-A3B and up to 7.6×\times on GLM-4-9B (Table III), with only gradual tapering before its own cliff as recomputed prompt share inches from 0.07 to 0.13.

Exact-length ablation and lossy comparison (Table III). Turning saved bytes into capacity requires exact-length objects. On AgentX KV, TileStream records average 0.710 of raw size (max 0.843), letting L1L_{1} hold 1.41×1.41\times as many objects; replacing exact-length allocation with 0.90-size fixed slots shrinks L1L_{1} gain to 1.11×1.11\times and drops 640 GB goodput from 13.5 to 8.4 req/min. Where accuracy loss is acceptable, lossy FP8 KV halves KV size and reaches 20.6 req/min at 640 GB (at the cost of altered outputs). Because LoomKV is lossless, it composes directly on top of FP8 KV: under DRAM-only serving at P=64P=64, raw FP8 KV overflows 400 GB DRAM (hit rate 0.61–0.75, goodput 6.6–10.6 req/min), and enabling tier mode lifts hit rate to 0.92 and goodput to 19.4 req/min.

VIII-E Q4: A compressed GPU pool

Once external tiers hold the full working set, GPU KV capacity becomes the sole bottleneck (Fig. 1b). Pool mode fits 1.31–1.34×\times as many KV tokens in the same GPU budget (Table IV), letting a node admit 12 concurrent long requests with roughly the queue and goodput of a raw pool at 8, while serving 1.16×\times as many prompt tokens per second.

Raising concurrency with ample tiers (Fig. 12, Table IV). All runs in Table IV use 400 GB DRAM and 2 TB SSD (0.93–0.94 hit rate throughout), isolating vLLM’s internal waiting queue. At S=8S=8, both pools run without queueing and serve similar goodput. Once admission rises to S=12S=12, the raw pool runs out of pages—tripling mean TTFT and dropping goodput sharply—whereas pool mode keeps waiting flat, delivers 1.5×\times raw’s goodput (matching raw’s best result at S=8S=8), and lifts prompt throughput by 1.16×\times over raw at S=8S=8 (1.11×\times over raw at S=12S=12). At S=16S=16, both pools queue, yet pool mode runs 14.0 concurrent requests against raw’s 11.1 and delivers 2.5×\times its goodput. GLM-4-9B exhibits the same shift one step higher, achieving 1.22×\times raw’s S=12S=12 throughput at S=16S=16 (Table IV).

Tighter GPU budget, page efficiency, and short tiers. Shared-budget pages yield 1.38×1.38\times raw blocks—versus 1.33×1.33\times if reserving the worst-case 2 KB per record and 1.42×1.42\times for ideal zero-slack packing. Deducting fixed backend buffers (staging buffers, overflow area, and record map) from the KV budget trims net token capacity only modestly, leaving 1.34×1.34\times usable tokens at 54 GB/GPU (≈2​–​3%\approx 2\text{--}3\% buffer share) and 1.31×1.31\times at 28 GB/GPU (≈4​–​5%\approx 4\text{--}5\% share). At 28 GB of KV per GPU, even S=8S=8 queues inside vLLM. Pool mode halves waiting and improves goodput by 1.8×\times over tier mode’s raw pool, matching a raw pool enlarged to the same token count (Tier, larger pool in Table IV) and confirming GPU-pool capacity equivalence. Raw LMCache is omitted at 28 GB because its runs stalled when a few loaded-but-unstarted long requests held 72–82% of the pool with no running request to preempt—a vLLM small-pool scheduling artifact. Finally, because pool mode exports FragPack records unchanged to L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, it also relieves short tiers: at 640 GB SSD (S=8S=8), it matches tier mode’s goodput (14.5 vs. 13.5 req/min) with 15% lower mean TTFT.

VIII-F Q5: A second workload

On a second workload where both the external tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier mode removes most of raw’s excess TTFT, and pool mode removes most of the remainder.

This trace replays an internal AI IDE service open-loop over three hours (5,098 requests at 0.47 req/s; mean prompt 68K, p99 192K; mean output 505 tokens) with no FIFO admission proxy, so TTFT directly includes vLLM queueing (Table V). On a constrained node (128 GB DRAM + 512 GB SSD), raw LMCache loses 7 percentage points of hit rate relative to a large raw reference (0.80 vs. 0.87 at 400 GB + 2 TB); recomputing those long prefixes saturates the GPUs, inflating mean queueing past 20 s and pushing ITL to 54 ms. Tier mode nearly restores total hit rate (0.86 vs. 0.87)—cutting mean TTFT by 5.6×\times and lifting goodput by 1.24×\times—but requests still queue as the GPU pool becomes the bottleneck. Pool mode relieves both levels at once: expanding GPU pool tokens shifts most hits directly into the GPU pool, slashing queueing wait and raising goodput by 1.59×\times over raw—outperforming even the large raw reference despite having one-third the DRAM and one-quarter the SSD (Table V).

VIII-G Q6: Costs and exactness

Where raw tiers already hold the working set, compression costs at most 2.2% of throughput. Tier mode produces outputs bit-identical to raw LMCache, while pool mode stores every KV bit losslessly and matches FA3’s numerical accuracy.

Overheads. Four system costs bound the price of compression: (1) GPU memory: tier mode uses about 2.5 GB more GPU memory per card than raw LMCache (2.1 GB for 32-chunk store and rotating load buffers). (2) Throughput with ample tiers: at equal hit rate and goodput, tier mode costs 1.3% throughput on DRAM-only (P=24P=24) and 2.2% on 2 TB SSD. (3) Zero-reuse store cost: on 320 unique 32K-token prompts with zero hits, end-to-end time grows by 0.3% in tier mode and 0.9% in pool mode. (4) GPU interference and compute share: running tier mode’s store and load paths at AgentX’s chunk rate beside an offline vLLM job slows vLLM by 1.5% (vs. 0.5% for raw copies) due to multi-process time slicing; in pool mode, FragPack compression takes 1.5% of GPU time against 48% for attention.

Tier mode: bit-exact outputs. GPU unit tests verify every decompressed block byte for byte across raw fallback, partial tiles, and corrupted headers. End to end, greedy decoding outputs with compressed tiers match raw-tier outputs by SHA-1 hash on both Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM-4-9B—key for reproducible evaluation, reinforcement-learning (RL) rollouts [29, 30], and safety-sensitive deployments where KV quantization degrades alignment [31].

Pool mode: lossless storage with a fused kernel. The fused decode kernel produces bitwise identical outputs over compressed and raw FragPack records, confirming zero coding error. Because the fused kernel accumulates attention outputs in a different floating-point summation order from FA3, final logits differ only at rounding precision: against an FP64 reference, mean absolute decode error matches FA3 (3.1×10−53.1\times 10^{-5} vs. 3.1×10−53.1\times 10^{-5} on BF16; 3.0×10−53.0\times 10^{-5} vs. 5.1×10−45.1\times 10^{-4} on FP8, where FA3 also quantizes queries). End-to-end accuracy agrees on GSM8K [32] and 32K–128K RULER [33] multi-key needles and five-hop variable tracking (within one standard error, paired McNemar p≥0.42p\geq 0.42), whereas vLLM’s lossy FP8 KV [34] misses needles that FA3 retrieves (p=0.03p=0.03, uncorrected).

IX Discussion

Both modes of LoomKV share the same lossless code; deciding which mode to enable depends on which level of the KV hierarchy exhausts capacity first, as observed from live serving metrics.

Choosing a mode. Our evaluation points to four operating regimes. (1) External tiers are the bottleneck: use tier mode. Observable signs are frequent SSD hits or a cache hit rate noticeably below that of unbounded tiers. Tier mode makes existing DRAM and SSD behave like 1.4×1.4\times larger raw tiers—delivering its largest gains near the LRU cliff—while preserving FA3’s exact output bits so model outputs need no re-qualification. (2) The GPU pool is the bottleneck: use pool mode. Observable signs are a high cache hit rate alongside a persistent waiting queue inside the inference engine. Here external tiers already fit the working set, so only compressing the GPU pool increases active concurrency; the fused decode kernel requires one-time validation, matching FA3 up to floating-point rounding. (3) Both levels are short: use pool mode. Because pool mode exports its FragPack records unchanged to L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, it expands both the GPU pool and the external tiers simultaneously, delivering the highest gains when both levels are constrained, as on our AI IDE workload. (4) Neither level is short: disable compression. When raw tiers and the raw pool already hold the working set without queueing, compression adds no capacity benefit and costs up to 2.2% of throughput. Across all cases, compression pays off most where physical capacity cannot simply be added—GPU memory, DRAM-only nodes, and nodes with fixed local NVMe—while saving storage hardware wherever SSD capacity is elastic.

Capacity sizing rule. Operators can size external tiers in two steps. First, estimate the active reused working set WW. Under LMCache’s write-through LRU, raw deployments clear the cliff once total DRAM plus SSD reaches roughly 1.8​W1.8W, or once DRAM alone reaches 1.2​–​1.3​W1.2\text{--}1.3W. Both multiples exceed WW because WW measures only the mean KV of live sessions, whereas LRU also retains expired chunks until they age out, and write-through duplicates hot chunks across both DRAM and SSD. Second, multiply this raw requirement by LoomKV’s stored ratio: compressed tiers need 0.71 of the raw DRAM and SSD capacity for BF16 KV, and 0.85–0.87 for FP8 KV.

Composing with replacement policies. Compression reduces the bytes per cached prefix without altering which prefixes a replacement policy chooses to retain, so the two compose orthogonally. To verify this, we replay the measured AgentX request traces through a cache simulator that models compression by scaling tier capacity by the inverse stored ratio (1/0.7091/0.709); this reproduces both measured LRU cliffs within 80 GB. Replacing LRU in the simulator confirms composition across policies. On DRAM alone, LRU over compressed records caches 0.81–0.92 of prompt tokens between the cliffs, surpassing even Belady’s optimal offline policy [35] over raw bytes (0.78–0.88). With DRAM plus SSD, replacing write-through LRU with a single exclusive LRU [36] (keeping each object in only one tier) shifts the raw cliff to fewer bytes—caching at most 0.29 of prompt tokens up to 720 GB and jumping to 0.88 at 840 GB—and compression shifts the exclusive-LRU cliff by the exact same 0.71 factor (reaching 0.87 hit rate at 600 GB). Thus, the replacement policy sets the baseline cliff location, and lossless compression consistently scales it down to 0.71 of the bytes.

Scope and limitations. Our evaluation covers single-node serving at TP 1 and TP 2 over PCIe. Each TP rank compresses, stores, and decompresses its own KV heads with their own per-head codebooks and no cross-GPU communication, so the stored ratio does not depend on the TP degree. Pipeline and expert parallelism, multi-engine shared cache servers, multi-head latent attention (MLA), and FP4 KV remain untested; for MLA, TileStream can compress latent vectors directly, whereas pool mode’s GQA kernel would need adaptation. In hybrid architectures mixing attention with linear or state-space layers, LoomKV compresses only attention KV layers. Pool mode’s current backend supports BF16 and FP8 KV, 128-dimension heads, GQA group sizes up to 8, and 128-token blocks. Finally, FP8 pool mode yields limited end-to-end gain for two reasons: shared pages must be sized for the hardest-to-compress layer (0.906 ratio versus 0.838 mean), and the FP8 fused kernel runs slower than FA3 at the power cap.

X Related Work

Tiered KV caches. LMCache [5], Mooncake [6], CachedAttention [8], SGLang HiCache [7], and Strata [9] offload uncompressed KV to DRAM and SSD to avoid repeated prefill. Tutti [37] accelerates SSD loading via GPU-initiated IO, whereas LoomKV increases how many prefixes fit in each tier. Placement [38] and replacement policies [39, 36, 35] decide which chunks to retain, whereas lossless compression shrinks each chunk and composes orthogonally with them.

Lossy KV compression. Quantization schemes such as CacheGen [11], KVTC [12], KIVI [10], KVQuant [40], FP8 KV [34], and PackKV [41], as well as token-eviction methods such as H2O [13] and SnapKV [14], save more space than lossless coding but alter KV values and model outputs; LoomKV preserves every bit and can also layer losslessly on top of quantized formats such as FP8 KV.

Lossless numerical compression. Beyond general-purpose GPU compressors (nvCOMP [19]), offline weight compressors (DFloat11 [20], ZipNN [21], ZipServ [17], and Heilper and Singer [42]), and transfer-oriented SplitZip [22] discussed in §II, several concurrent systems target lossless KV coding. ExANS [26] encodes paged BF16 exponents with ANS (Table II), achieving a slightly lower ratio than LoomKV but decompressing 6.3×\times slower and lacking fixed lane offsets for fused attention. AdaCode [43] achieves a 0.72 average BF16 KV ratio. From database storage, PFOR [44] packs fixed-width codes with out-of-band exceptions, ALP-RD [25] pairs a 3-bit leading-bit dictionary with exceptions, and Parquet’s byte-stream-split [45] separates bytes by position as TileStream does; LoomKV combines a two-level 3-bit escape code with a lane-parallel GPU layout akin to FastLanes [46].

Fused attention over compressed KV. Quantized attention kernels dequantize on the fly, and ZipServ fuses decompression into weight GEMMs. Concurrent ZipFusion [27] decompresses BF16 KV inside FlashInfer decode attention at a 0.79 ratio (Table II) without external tiers. Concurrent GAAC [47] targets personal devices with calibrated per-channel exponent codes (0.712 stored ratio, i.e., 1.405×\times capacity, on BF16), a fused kernel, and fixed slots; LoomKV targets multi-request serving engines, pools variable-length budgets across page records, integrates with tiered storage, and tightens FP8 KV (0.85–0.87 vs. 0.88–0.92).

Compressed buffer management. OS compression caches such as Douglis [48] and zswap [49] interpose a compressed tier ahead of slower storage, flash caches such as CacheLib [50] and Kangaroo [51] manage variable-length SSD objects, and database engines such as InnoDB [52] and Umbra [53] pack or resize compressed pages; LoomKV brings exact-length tier allocation and shared-budget compressed GPU pages to unmodified LLM serving stacks.

XI Conclusion

We presented LoomKV, a lossless KV cache compression system spanning both external cache tiers (DRAM and SSD) and the GPU KV pool without modifying the inference engine. Built on a calibrated two-level 3-bit high-byte code, LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and turns those savings into capacity via exact-length tier objects (TileStream) and shared-budget compressed GPU pages (FragPack), paired with branchless direct-to-page decompression, fused decode attention, and stall-free asynchronous transfers. On AgentX, compressed tiers act as raw tiers with 1.4×1.4\times the capacity—delivering 2.7–3.6×\times raw’s goodput across LMCache’s LRU cliff—while a compressed GPU pool admits 12 long requests with roughly the queue and goodput of a raw pool at 8. On an AI IDE workload where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier mode and pool mode lift goodput by 1.24×\times and 1.59×\times, respectively. Where raw capacity already suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% of throughput; tier mode preserves bit-identical outputs, and pool mode matches FA3 up to floating-point rounding.
